title: Find the Duplicate Number
directAnswer: Treat the array as a linked list where index i points to nums[i]. Because values are in [1, n] and there are n+1 of them, a duplicate creates a cycle. Run Floyd's tortoise-and-hare to find the cycle, then the cycle entrance is the duplicate — O(n) time, O(1) space, and the array is left unmodified.

remember.pattern: Array as implicit linked list + Floyd's cycle detection (tortoise & hare)
remember.formula:
slow = fast = nums[0]
repeat: slow = nums[slow]; fast = nums[nums[fast]]  until slow == fast
slow2 = nums[0]
while slow2 != slow: slow = nums[slow]; slow2 = nums[slow2]
return slow
rules: The mapping `i → nums[i]` is a valid linked list because every value is in `[1, n]`, so it's always a legal index (never points out of bounds, never to index 0 from itself in a way that breaks the start).
Start both pointers at `nums[0]` (or conceptually at index 0 then take one step). The duplicate is the **entrance** of the cycle, not just any node in it.
Phase 1 finds a meeting point inside the cycle; Phase 2 resets one pointer to the start and walks both at speed 1 — they meet at the entrance. This is Floyd's, not random.
This does **not** modify the array and uses **O(1)** space — that's the whole reason it beats the sort and the seen-set.
It finds the duplicate *value*, not its index, and works even if the duplicate appears more than twice.
whenToUse: Values are confined to [1, n] with n+1 elements → a cycle is guaranteed
You're forbidden from modifying the array AND must use O(1) extra space
You recognize 'each element points to another index' as a linked-list traversal
Exactly one duplicated value (possibly repeated) is promised
antiSignals: You're allowed O(n) extra space → a hash set is simpler and just as fast
You're allowed to sort / mutate → sort then scan adjacent, or index-marking, is easier to code
Values aren't bounded to [1, n] → the linked-list framing breaks; use hashing
remember.takeaway: The leap is seeing an array of bounded values as a linked list whose cycle entrance is the duplicate. Once you reframe it that way, Floyd's algorithm delivers O(n) time and O(1) space without touching the input — the exact constraint combo interviewers use to rule out the easy answers.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can reframe a bounded-value array as a linked list and apply Floyd's two-phase cycle detection to hit O(1) space without mutating the input.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reaching for a hash set or sort (violating the no-extra-space / no-modify constraints), or running only phase 1 and returning the meeting point instead of the cycle entrance.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain why a cycle must exist (pigeonhole on values in [1, n]), then derive why phase 2 lands exactly on the entrance — the algebra of the distances, not hand-waving.

problemStatement:
Given an array `nums` of `n + 1` integers where each value is in the range `[1, n]`, there is exactly one repeated number. Return that repeated number.

You must **not modify** the array and must use only **constant** extra space, in better than O(n²) time.
constraints: 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ n (every value is a valid index into nums)
Exactly one value is duplicated; it may appear more than twice
understanding: Because n+1 values are drawn from {1..n}, the pigeonhole principle guarantees a repeat. Reading nums[i] as 'next pointer from node i' turns the array into a linked list with a cycle, and the duplicate is precisely where the cycle begins.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I modify the array or use extra space?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraints say no to both. That rules out sorting and a hash set and points to the Floyd's-on-the-array approach.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the duplicate appear more than twice?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Floyd's still works — multiple occurrences just mean multiple edges into the cycle entrance, which is still the answer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are all values guaranteed in [1, n]?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's what makes nums[i] always a legal index and the linked-list framing valid. If values could be 0 or out of range, this breaks.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want the value or an index?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The duplicated value. The cycle entrance node's identifier is exactly that value.

examples.explanation: 2 appears twice. Following indices 0→1→3→2→4→2→4… cycles at 2.
3 is repeated; the implicit linked list's cycle entrance is 3.

approaches.name: Hash Set (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Offer it first as the obvious O(n)-time idea, then note it violates the O(1)-space rule and pivot.
hints: What's the simplest way to detect the first value you've already seen?
Walk the array, adding each value to a set; the first value already present is the duplicate.
This is O(n) time but O(n) space — and the problem forbids extra space. How could you detect a repeat without storing seen values?
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass with O(1) average set operations → O(n) time. The set can hold up to n values → O(n) space, which the constraints disallow.
approaches.explanation:
Scan the array, inserting each value into a hash set. The moment you try to insert a value that's already there, that value is the duplicate.

**Why it's the natural first answer.** 'Find the repeated element' screams 'remember what you've seen', and a hash set gives O(1) membership. It's correct, simple, and a good baseline to state.

**Why it fails the constraints.** The problem explicitly caps extra space at O(1), and the set grows to O(n). So while the time is optimal, the space disqualifies it. Mentioning it shows you know the easy route and understand precisely which rule rules it out — a better signal than pretending the constraint isn't there.

**The bridge to the real answer.** To drop the space to O(1) without mutating the array, you need structure already present in the data. The clue is the value range `[1, n]`: every element is itself a valid index, which means the array can be *read* as a linked list — and detecting a repeat becomes detecting a cycle, which Floyd's does in O(1) space.
approaches.insight: The hash set trades space for simplicity. When an interviewer forbids that space, look for exploitable structure in the input — here, values being valid indices is the door to the pointer-chasing solution.

dryRun.intro: Insert each value; stop at the first already in the set.

Returning the index instead of the value.
Assuming it generalizes when values aren't in [1, n] — it does, but the optimal doesn't.

approaches.name: Floyd's Cycle Detection on the Array (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want under the no-modify, O(1)-space constraints. Frame the array as a linked list first.
hints: Read nums[i] as 'the next index to jump to from i'. Since every value is in [1, n], that's always a valid jump. What shape does following the jumps trace out?
Because two indices share the same value (the duplicate), two arrows point into the same node — that creates a cycle. Finding the duplicate becomes finding the cycle's entrance.

Phase 1: tortoise (one step) and hare (two steps) until they meet inside the cycle. Phase 2: reset one pointer to nums[0], advance both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle entrance, which is the duplicate.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Phase 1 and phase 2 each traverse O(n) nodes before meeting (the pointers cover at most a constant multiple of the list length). No auxiliary storage beyond two index variables → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Reinterpret the array as a function `f(i) = nums[i]`, i.e. a linked list where node `i` links to node `nums[i]`. Then run Floyd's two-phase cycle detection; the cycle's entrance node is the duplicated value.

**Why a cycle must exist.** There are `n + 1` slots but values only range over `{1, …, n}`, so by the pigeonhole principle some value repeats. In the linked-list view, a repeated value means two different nodes both link *to* the same node — two arrows converging. Following links forward from index `0` can therefore never escape to infinity; it must eventually revisit a node, i.e. loop. The starting index `0` is not part of the cycle (nothing points to it as a target since values are ≥ 1 and we begin there), so it sits on the 'tail' leading into the loop — exactly the linked-list-with-a-cycle shape Floyd's was designed for.

**Phase 1 — find a meeting point.** Move `slow` one step (`slow = nums[slow]`) and `fast` two steps (`fast = nums[nums[fast]]`). Inside a cycle the fast pointer gains one position on the slow pointer each iteration, so it eventually laps and lands on it. When `slow == fast`, you're guaranteed to be *somewhere inside* the cycle — but not necessarily at its entrance.

**Phase 2 — why resetting finds the entrance.** Let `a` be the distance from the start to the cycle entrance, `b` the distance from the entrance to the meeting point, and `c` the rest of the cycle (so the cycle length is `b + c`). When they meet, slow has walked `a + b` and fast has walked `a + b + k(b + c)` for some integer `k`; since fast moved twice as far, `2(a + b) = a + b + k(b + c)`, which simplifies to `a = (k−1)(b+c) + c`. In words: the distance from the start to the entrance equals the distance from the meeting point to the entrance (modulo whole loops). So if you put one pointer back at `nums[0]` and advance both one step at a time, they collide exactly at the entrance — the duplicate.

**Why this beats the alternatives.** It's O(n) time like the hash set but O(1) space, and unlike sorting it never touches the array. That precise combination — fast, constant space, read-only — is why interviewers pose this problem: it filters for candidates who can see the hidden linked-list structure rather than reach for the default tools.

**Why duplicates-more-than-twice are fine.** Extra occurrences just add more arrows into the cycle entrance; the entrance node is unchanged, so the algorithm still returns it.
approaches.insight: The entire trick is the reframe: a bounded-value array *is* a linked list, a duplicate *is* a cycle, and the duplicate value *is* the cycle entrance. Floyd's then gives O(1) space for free. The phase-2 reset working is a clean distance-algebra result, not magic — be ready to derive `a = c (mod cycle)`.

code.python:
def find_duplicate(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
    # Phase 1: find a meeting point inside the cycle
    slow = nums[0]
    fast = nums[nums[0]]
    while slow != fast:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]
    # Phase 2: find the cycle entrance = the duplicate
    slow = nums[0]
    while slow != fast:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[fast]
    return slow

Phase 2: reset one pointer to the start. The distance algebra makes both meet at the entrance.

pitfalls: Returning the phase-1 meeting point instead of running phase 2 to the entrance.
Mis-stepping the hare: it must be nums[nums[fast]], a true double step.
Assuming index 0 can be inside the cycle — it's on the tail because values are ≥ 1.
Falling back to a set or sort and violating the stated constraints.

commonMistakes: Using a hash set or sorting, violating the O(1)-space / no-modify constraints.
Returning the phase-1 meeting point instead of the cycle entrance.
Single-stepping the fast pointer instead of double-stepping.
Forgetting the array can be read as a linked list because values are in [1, n].

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Stopping at the meeting point
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Phase 1 only guarantees a node inside the cycle, not the entrance. You must run phase 2 (reset + equal-speed walk) to reach the duplicate.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while (slow != fast) { slow = nums[slow]; fast = nums[nums[fast]]; }
return slow;   // meeting point, NOT the entrance

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Fast pointer not double-stepping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The hare must advance twice per iteration (nums[nums[fast]]). Single-stepping makes both pointers identical and they never meaningfully meet inside the cycle.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Violating the constraints with a set
commonMistakesDetailed.why: It's correct but uses O(n) space, which the problem forbids. Under the stated rules, Floyd's is the expected answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
slow = fast = nums[0]
# ... Floyd's two-phase cycle detection in O(1) space

patternNote: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare applied to an array reinterpreted as a linked list. The transferable insight: when values are bounded to valid indices, i → nums[i] is a traversal, duplicates become cycles, and constant-space cycle detection replaces hashing. The phase-2 reset relies on the distance identity a ≡ c (mod cycle length).
